module.title: Recognising phishing
module.summary: What phishing is, the warning signs agencies highlight, and why a clean-looking email still deserves care.

blocks.title: Recognising phishing
blocks.body: Phishing emails are designed to look ordinary. In this module you will learn the signs that should make you pause — and why they are prompts to check rather than proof.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: What phishing is
blocks.body:
A **phishing** email imitates someone you trust — a colleague, a supplier, a bank or an internal IT team — to get you to click a link, open an attachment or hand over information.

The goal is almost always one of three things: your password, a payment, or a foothold on your device.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: Five signs worth checking
blocks.body:
National cyber-security agencies point to the same small set of warning signs:

- an **unexpected request** for credentials, payment or personal data
- **urgency or threats**, such as deadlines or account closure
- a **sender** whose display name and real address do not match
- a **link** whose text and real destination differ
- a **generic greeting** or tone that feels unlike the sender

blocks.title: A clean-looking email is not a safe email
blocks.body: Well-crafted phishing can show few or none of these signs. Treat the signs as reasons to **verify**, not as a checklist that clears a message when nothing is ticked.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: Spot the signs
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

interaction.stem: An email from “IT Service Desk” says your password expires in 30 minutes and asks you to sign in through the link. The sender address is it-desk@secure-helpdesk.net. Which signs are present? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sender address that does not match the organisation

interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right: the deadline, the sign-in request and the outside domain are all warning signs.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again: there is no attachment, but the deadline, the sign-in request and the outside domain are all signs.

optionFeedback.text: The message contains a link, not an attachment.

interaction.rationale: Three of the five agency-highlighted signs are present.

blocks.title: Signal or not?
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

options.text: The email asks you to confirm payroll bank details urgently
The email uses your manager’s usual sign-off
The link text shows the intranet but points elsewhere

interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A familiar sign-off is easy to copy, so it does not prove the email is genuine.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Remember: familiar details can be copied; they are not proof that a message is safe.
interaction.rationale: Attackers imitate familiar details; only independent verification settles doubt.

textEquivalent.short: Table of five phishing warning signs and what to look for
textEquivalent.long: Five warning signs: an unexpected request for credentials, payment or personal data; urgency or threats such as deadlines or account closure; a sender display name that does not match the real address; link text that does not match the real destination; and a generic greeting or unusual tone.

glossary.definition: A message that imitates a trusted sender to trick the recipient into an unsafe action.
Disguising a message’s sender or link so it appears to come from someone else.
